notes.front: What is a standard terminal arrival (STAR)?
notes.back: An ATC coded IFR arrival route for arriving IFR aircraft bound for certain airports.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual says STARs simplify clearance delivery and ease the transition from en route flight to instrument approach procedures.
notes.example: Like a signposted slip road off a motorway, but in the sky: it leads arriving traffic from the airways towards the approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: A STAR is an ATC coded IFR arrival route established for application to arriving IFR aircraft destined for certain airports. STARs simplify clearance delivery procedures, and also facilitate transition between en route and instrument approach procedures.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a descend via clearance authorise on a STAR?
notes.back: Descent at the pilot's discretion to meet the published restrictions, and lateral navigation along the STAR.
notes.explanation: The pilot chooses when to start down, but each published restriction on the arrival must still be met.
notes.example: Like being handed a hill-walk route card with spot heights, but you choose your own pace down as long as you reach each point at its height.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: Descend at pilot's discretion to meet published restrictions and laterally navigate on a STAR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is an instrument approach procedure (IAP)?
notes.back: A series of predetermined manoeuvres by reference to flight instruments, with specified obstacle protection and assured navigation signal reception.
notes.explanation: The definition starts it at the initial approach fix or, where one applies, at the beginning of a defined arrival route.
notes.example: Like a staircase with a handrail in the dark, but every step, turn and height is published and checked against obstacles.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Instrument approach procedure (IAP) is a series of predetermined maneuvers by reference to flight instruments with specified protection from obstacles and assurance of navigation signal reception capability. It begins from the initial approach fix, or where applicable, from the beginning of a defined arrival route to a point:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is an initial approach fix (IAF)?
notes.back: The fix where the initial approach segment begins.
notes.explanation: Part 97 runs the initial segment from the IAF to the intermediate fix, or to where the aircraft is established on the intermediate or final course.
notes.example: Like the start line of a marked trail, but for an approach: the fix where the initial segment begins.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Initial approach is the segment between the initial approach fix and the intermediate fix or the point where the aircraft is established on the intermediate course or final approach course.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a final approach fix (FAF)?
notes.back: The fix that begins the final approach segment, where final segment descent may begin.
notes.explanation: Crossing it marks the start of the last segment of the approach, the one flown down towards the minimums.
notes.example: Like the last checkpoint before the finishing straight, but it is where the final descent may start.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Final approach fix (FAF) defines the beginning of the final approach segment and the point where final segment descent may begin.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a procedure turn?
notes.back: The manoeuvre prescribed to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course.
notes.explanation: Its job is course reversal: getting the aircraft pointed inbound on the approach course.
notes.example: Like a three-point turn in a signed turning area, but flown within a charted distance of a fix.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn
notes.evidence: A procedure turn is the maneuver prescribed when it is necessary to reverse direction to establish the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a hold in lieu of procedure turn?
notes.back: A holding pattern, set up under FAA criteria, flown instead of a procedure turn to reverse course.
notes.explanation: Part 97 treats it as another way of doing the course reversal that a procedure turn would otherwise do.
notes.example: Like going once round a roundabout to come back the way you came, but as a published racetrack pattern at a fix.
introduces: hold in lieu of procedure turn
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Hold in lieu of PT means a holding pattern established under applicable FAA criteria, and used in lieu of a procedure turn to execute a course reversal.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
uses: hold in lieu of procedure turn

notes.front: What is a terminal arrival area (TAA)?
notes.back: A transition from the en route structure to the terminal area for area navigation aircraft, with minimum altitudes giving standard obstacle clearance.
notes.explanation: It is designed to need little pilot and controller interface: inside its boundaries the charted altitudes already give obstacle clearance.
notes.example: Like pie slices drawn round a town, each labelled with a safe height, but tied to the initial fixes of one approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: The TAA provides a transition from the en route structure to the terminal environment with little required pilot/air traffic control interface for aircraft equipped with Area Navigation (RNAV) systems. A TAA provides minimum altitudes with standard obstacle clearance when operating within the TAA boundaries.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a decision altitude (DA)?
notes.back: The altitude, in feet above mean sea level, at which the pilot must continue the approach or immediately start a missed approach.
notes.explanation: The choice turns on whether the required visual reference is in sight on reaching it.
notes.example: Like a motorway junction where you must commit to one road, but reached by altimeter reading instead of a sign.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Decision altitude (DA) is a specified altitude in an instrument approach procedure at which the pilot must decide whether to initiate an immediate missed approach if the pilot does not see the required visual reference, or to continue the approach. Decision altitude is expressed in feet above mean sea level.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a decision height (DH)?
notes.back: The same continue-or-miss decision point, but specified as a height in feet above ground level.
notes.explanation: It works like a DA, restated as a height above the ground instead of an altitude.
notes.example: Like measuring a shelf from the floor instead of from sea level, but for the decision point on an approach.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Decision height (DH) is a specified height above the ground in an instrument approach procedure at which the pilot must decide whether to initiate an immediate missed approach
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a minimum descent altitude (MDA)?
notes.back: The lowest MSL altitude to which descent is authorised on final or while circling, until the required visual references are seen.
notes.explanation: It is a floor, not a decision point: going below it waits until the pilot sees the references for the runway.
notes.example: Like a ledge you must stay on until you can see the path down, but on an approach it holds until the runway references are in sight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Minimum descent altitude (MDA) is the lowest altitude specified in an instrument approach procedure, expressed in feet above mean sea level, to which descent is authorized on final approach or during circle-to-land maneuvering until the pilot sees the required visual references for the heliport or runway of intended landing.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is height above touchdown (HAT)?
notes.back: How high a minimum sits above the touchdown zone elevation, as a height instead of an altitude above sea level.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines it among the symbols and terms used in approach procedures.
notes.example: Like giving a diving board height from the pool surface, not from sea level, but for how high a minimum sits above the landing zone.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: HAT means height above touchdown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a precision approach procedure under section 1.1 of the regulations?
notes.back: A standard instrument approach procedure that provides an electronic glide slope, such as an ILS.
notes.explanation: The electronic glide slope is the test: the regulation names the ILS and precision approach radar as examples.
notes.example: Like a ramp with a rail for both direction and slope, but built from radio signals.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Precision approach procedure means a standard instrument approach procedure in which an electronic glide slope is provided, such as ILS and PAR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a nonprecision approach procedure under section 1.1 of the regulations?
notes.back: A standard instrument approach procedure in which no electronic glide slope is provided.
notes.explanation: The definition turns only on the missing electronic glide slope, whatever lateral guidance the procedure uses.
notes.example: Like a ramp with a side rail but nothing to show the slope, but in the air: lateral guidance only.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Nonprecision approach procedure means a standard instrument approach procedure in which no electronic glide slope is provided.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is an approach with vertical guidance (APV)?
notes.back: An approach giving course and glidepath guidance from a system not required to meet the international precision approach standards.
notes.explanation: It gives vertical guidance like a precision approach while falling outside the precision standard.
notes.example: Like a ramp with a slope rail that is not certified to the strictest standard, but still gives you a path down.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Approach with Vertical Guidance (APV). An instrument approach based on a navigation system that is not required to meet the precision approach standards of ICAO Annex 10 but provides course and glidepath deviation information.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is localizer performance with vertical guidance (LPV)?
notes.back: A line of minima on area navigation (GPS) approaches using WAAS lateral and vertical guidance, very similar to a Category I ILS.
notes.explanation: The improved accuracy of WAAS is what lets these approaches come so close to an ILS.
notes.example: Like an ILS built from satellite signals instead of ground transmitters, but shown as one line in the minimums box.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: “LPV” is the acronym for localizer performance with vertical guidance. RNAV (GPS) approaches to LPV lines of minima take advantage of the improved accuracy of WAAS lateral and vertical guidance to provide an approach that is very similar to a Category I Instrument Landing System (ILS).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is LNAV/VNAV?
notes.back: Approach with vertical guidance minimums for an area navigation approach, usually flown with approach-certified barometric vertical navigation.
notes.explanation: Its lateral and vertical integrity limits are larger than those of a precision approach or LPV.
notes.example: Like LPV's cousin, but its glidepath is often worked out from the altimeter instead of satellites.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: LNAV/VNAV identifies APV minimums developed to accommodate an RNAV IAP with vertical guidance, usually provided by approach certified Baro-VNAV, but with lateral and vertical integrity limits larger than a precision approach or LPV.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are lateral navigation (LNAV) minimums?
notes.back: Minimums for lateral navigation only, published as a minimum descent altitude.
notes.explanation: With no vertical guidance on this line, its minimum is an MDA instead of a DA.
notes.example: Like following a painted centre line with nothing to show the slope, but on a GPS approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: LNAV. This minima is for lateral navigation only, and the approach minimum altitude will be published as a minimum descent altitude (MDA).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is localizer performance (LP)?
notes.back: A WAAS line of minima with lateral guidance that grows more sensitive near the runway, like a localizer, but no vertical guidance.
notes.explanation: Angular guidance here means increasing lateral sensitivity close to the runway, not a glideslope angle.
notes.example: Like a localizer drawn by satellites, but still with no glide path to follow.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: “LP” is the acronym for localizer performance. Approaches to LP lines of minima take advantage of the improved accuracy of WAAS to provide approaches, with lateral guidance and angular guidance. Angular guidance does not refer to a glideslope angle but rather to the increased lateral sensitivity as the aircraft gets closer to the runway, similar to localizer approaches.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a visual descent point (VDP)?
notes.back: A defined point on the final course of a nonprecision straight-in approach from which a stabilised visual descent from the MDA may begin.
notes.explanation: It marks where a normal visual descent from the MDA to the touchdown point can start.
notes.example: Like the brow of a hill where the car park comes into view and you start down, but for leaving the MDA.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Visual Descent Point (VDP), identified by the symbol (V), is a defined point on the final approach course of a nonprecision straight-in approach procedure from which a stabilized visual descent from the MDA to the runway touchdown point may be commenced.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a stabilised approach?
notes.back: One flown with a constant approach speed, descent rate, vertical flight path and configuration in its final stages.
notes.explanation: Holding these steady in the last stages of the approach is what the handbook calls the stabilised approach concept.
notes.example: Like a train rolling into a platform at a steady pace and angle, but set up in three dimensions well before the runway.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: constant approach speed, descent rate, vertical flight path,
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is runway visual range (RVR), as used in approach minimums?
notes.back: A visibility value in feet measured by instruments along the runway.
notes.explanation: Older systems measure it with transmissometers on towers along the runway; newer ones use forward scatter sensors. Values are given in feet.
notes.example: Like a light meter judging fog down a corridor, but it tells a pilot how far along the runway the lights can be seen.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 7-1-13 Runway Visual Range (RVR)
notes.evidence: RVR values are measured by transmissometers mounted on 14-foot towers along the runway.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a no-gyro approach?
notes.back: A radar approach or vectors for a pilot whose directional gyro or other stabilised compass is inoperative or inaccurate.
notes.explanation: The pilot advises ATC of the failure and asks for no-gyro vectors or an approach.
notes.example: Like a sat-nav voice saying "turn left… stop" when your compass has failed, but from a radar controller.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-11 Radar Approaches
notes.evidence: This approach is available to a pilot under radar control who experiences circumstances wherein the directional gyro or other stabilized compass is inoperative or inaccurate. When this occurs, the pilot should so advise ATC and request a No-Gyro vector or approach.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are timed approaches from a holding fix?
notes.back: Approaches in which each pilot in the sequence is given a time to leave the holding fix inbound.
notes.explanation: The pilot adjusts the flight path to leave the fix as close as possible to the time given.
notes.example: Like trains leaving a station on a timetable, but aircraft leaving a holding fix at assigned minutes.
introduces: timed approaches from a holding fix
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-10 Timed Approaches from a Holding Fix
notes.evidence: Each pilot in an approach sequence will be given advance notice as to the time they should leave the holding point on approach to the airport. When a time to leave the holding point has been received, the pilot should adjust the flight path to leave the fix as closely as possible to the designated time.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
uses: timed approaches from a holding fix

notes.front: What is a side-step manoeuvre?
notes.back: An approach to one of two parallel runways 1,200 feet apart or less, followed by a straight-in landing on the other runway.
notes.explanation: ATC authorises it, clearing the approach to one runway and the landing on its neighbour.
notes.example: Like changing lanes just before a motorway exit, but from one parallel runway's approach to the runway beside it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-19 Side-step Maneuver
notes.evidence: ATC may authorize a standard instrument approach procedure which serves either one of parallel runways that are separated by 1,200 feet or less followed by a straight-in landing on the adjacent runway.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are simultaneous parallel approaches?
notes.back: Instrument approaches flown at the same time to dual or triple parallel runways, in classes such as dependent and independent.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual sorts these operations into three classes instead of treating every parallel approach alike.
notes.example: Like two lanes of traffic merging side by side at a toll plaza, but aircraft flying to neighbouring runways at once.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-13 Simultaneous Approaches to Parallel Runways
notes.evidence: ATC procedures permit ILS/RNAV/GLS instrument approach operations to dual or triple parallel runway configurations. ILS/RNAV/GLS approaches to parallel runways are grouped into three classes: Simultaneous Dependent Approaches; Simultaneous Independent Approaches; and Simultaneous Close Parallel PRM Approaches.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is an RNP authorization required (RNP AR) procedure?
notes.back: An approach or departure procedure that every operator needs specific FAA authorisation to fly.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual likens it to the special authorisation needed for Category II or III ILS procedures.
notes.example: Like a black ski run that needs a special pass, but for tightly designed satellite approaches.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-18 RNP AR (Authorization Required) Instrument Procedures
notes.evidence: RNP AR procedures require authorization analogous to the special authorization required for Category II or III ILS procedures. All operators require specific authorization from the FAA to fly any RNP AR approach or departure procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a STAR, are published 'expect' altitudes and speeds crossing restrictions?
notes.back: No, not unless ATC issues them verbally.
notes.explanation: Only a verbal ATC instruction turns an 'expect' value into something the pilot must meet.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: “Expect” altitudes/speeds are not considered STAR procedures crossing restrictions unless verbally issued by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Published speed restrictions on a STAR are independent of altitude restrictions and are {{c1::mandatory unless modified by ATC}}.
notes.back: Mandatory unless modified by ATC.
notes.explanation: Because the two kinds are independent, an instruction about altitude leaves a published speed in force.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: Published speed restrictions are independent of altitude restrictions and are mandatory unless modified by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a pilot assume when vectored or cleared to deviate off a STAR?
notes.back: That the STAR is cancelled, together with its published altitude and speed restrictions.
notes.explanation: The cancellation covers the published restrictions as well as the route.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: If vectored or cleared to deviate off a STAR, pilots must consider the STAR canceled. If the STAR contains published altitude restrictions, speed restrictions, or a chart note used to transition from Mach to IAS, those restrictions are also canceled
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Descending via a STAR, what must the pilot say on first contact with each new frequency?
notes.back: The altitude leaving and 'descending via' the procedure name, plus any assigned runway transition and unpublished restrictions.
notes.explanation: The rule applies at each frequency change during the descent, not only the first.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: Pilots cleared for vertical navigation using the phraseology “descend via” must inform ATC upon initial contact with a new frequency, of the altitude leaving, “descending via (procedure name),” the runway transition or landing direction if assigned, and any assigned restrictions not published on the procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which approach segment runs from the initial approach fix to the intermediate fix?
notes.back: The initial approach segment.
notes.explanation: Part 97 also lets it end where the aircraft is established on the intermediate or final approach course.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Initial approach is the segment between the initial approach fix and the intermediate fix or the point where the aircraft is established on the intermediate course or final approach course.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which approach segment lies between the intermediate fix and the final approach fix?
notes.back: The intermediate approach segment.
notes.explanation: It joins the initial segment to the final one; its far end is the FAF.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Intermediate approach is the segment between the intermediate fix or point and the final approach fix.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where does the final approach segment end?
notes.back: At the runway, the airport or the missed approach point.
notes.explanation: Its start is the final approach fix or point; which end applies depends on the procedure.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Final approach is the segment between the final approach fix or point and the runway, airport, or missed approach point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which segment runs from the missed approach point, or arrival at DA/DH, to the missed approach fix?
notes.back: The missed approach segment.
notes.explanation: It is the one segment that begins at a decision point and ends at a fix reached at a prescribed altitude.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Missed approach is the segment between the missed approach point, or point of arrival at decision altitude or decision height (DA/DH), and the missed approach fix at the prescribed altitude.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When an instrument approach to a civil airport is necessary, what must be used unless the FAA authorises otherwise?
notes.back: A standard instrument approach procedure prescribed in part 97 for that airport.
notes.explanation: The paragraph exempts only United States military aircraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized by the FAA, when it is necessary to use an instrument approach to a civil airport, each person operating an aircraft must use a standard instrument approach procedure prescribed in part 97 of this chapter for that airport. This paragraph does not apply to United States military aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying a civil aircraft under IFR into a military airport, whose approach procedures and minimums apply?
notes.back: Those prescribed by the military authority having jurisdiction of that airport, unless the Administrator prescribes otherwise.
notes.explanation: The part 97 civil procedures are not the reference there; the military authority sets them.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (g)
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise prescribed by the Administrator, each person operating a civil aircraft under IFR into or out of a military airport shall comply with the instrument approach procedures and the takeoff and landing minimum prescribed by the military authority having jurisdiction of that airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When a procedure turn is depicted on the approach chart, when may the pilot leave it out?
notes.back: When cleared straight-in, when arriving on a NoPT route or sector, when radar vectored to final, or on a timed approach.
notes.explanation: A depicted course reversal is part of the approach, so it is flown unless something removes it: a straight-in clearance, a NoPT route, or a radar vector or timed approach, when it needs ATC clearance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn
notes.evidence: The procedure turn or hold-in-lieu-of-PT is a required maneuver when it is depicted on the approach chart, unless cleared by ATC for a straight-in approach.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The altitude prescribed for the procedure turn is a {{c1::minimum}} altitude until the aircraft is established on the inbound course.
notes.back: Minimum.
notes.explanation: Descent below it waits until the aircraft is inbound on the approach course.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn
notes.evidence: The altitude prescribed for the procedure turn is a minimum altitude until the aircraft is established on the inbound course.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What maximum speed should be observed from first crossing the course reversal IAF through the procedure turn?
notes.back: Not greater than 200 knots indicated airspeed.
notes.explanation: The limit keeps the turn inside the obstruction clearance area.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-9 Procedure Turn and Hold-in-lieu of Procedure Turn
notes.evidence: a maximum speed of not greater than 200 knots (IAS) should be observed from first overheading the course reversal IAF through the procedure turn maneuver to ensure containment within the obstruction clearance area.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(j), in which cases may no pilot make a procedure turn unless cleared by ATC?
notes.back: A radar vector to the final approach course or fix, a timed approach from a holding fix, or a procedure marked NoPT.
notes.explanation: The rule is a limitation: in these cases a course reversal needs its own ATC clearance.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (j)
notes.evidence: In the case of a radar vector to a final approach course or fix, a timed approach from a holding fix, or an approach for which the procedure specifies “No PT,” no pilot may make a procedure turn unless cleared to do so by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
uses: timed approaches from a holding fix

notes.front: How much obstacle clearance do TAA altitudes give, and how do they differ from minimum safe altitudes?
notes.back: At least 1,000 feet, more in mountains; unlike minimum safe altitudes, they are operationally usable.
notes.explanation: On charts with a TAA they take the place of the minimum safe altitude.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Altitudes published within the TAA replace the MSA altitude. However, unlike MSA altitudes the TAA altitudes are operationally usable altitudes. These altitudes provide at least 1,000 feet of obstacle clearance, more in mountainous areas.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does a pilot tell which TAA area the aircraft will enter?
notes.back: From the magnetic bearing to the dual-purpose intermediate fix/IAF, compared with the published boundary bearings.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual warns against using the bearing to the left-base or right-base IAFs.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: The pilot can determine which area of the TAA the aircraft will enter by determining the magnetic bearing of the aircraft TO the fix labeled IF/IAF. The bearing should then be compared to the published lateral boundary bearings that define the TAA areas. Do not use magnetic bearing to the right-base or left-base IAFs to determine position.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Does a clearance direct to an IAF in a TAA, without an approach clearance, allow descent to a lower TAA altitude?
notes.back: No; the pilot must ask ATC for the lower TAA altitude.
notes.explanation: A direct-to clearance changes only the route, not the altitude the aircraft may descend to.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: An ATC clearance direct to an IAF or to the IF/IAF without an approach clearance does not authorize a pilot to descend to a lower TAA altitude. If a pilot desires a lower altitude without an approach clearance, request the lower TAA altitude from ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Radar vectored and cleared for the approach, what altitude does the pilot keep?
notes.back: The last assigned altitude, until established on a segment of a published route or the approach.
notes.explanation: Once established, the published altitudes for each following segment govern the descent.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: maintain the last assigned altitude unless a different altitude is assigned by ATC, or until the aircraft is established on a segment of a published route or IAP. After the aircraft is so established, published altitudes apply to descent within each succeeding route or approach segment unless a different altitude is assigned by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: ATC says 'cleared approach' without naming a procedure. What may the pilot fly?
notes.back: Any one of the authorised instrument approach procedures for that airport, but not a contact or visual approach.
notes.explanation: The clearance may come with a route to or over an IAF or feeder fix.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-6 Approach Clearance
notes.evidence: This clearance indicates the pilot may execute any one of the authorized IAPs for that airport. The clearance may be issued in conjunction with the route to or over an IAF or feeder fix. This clearance does not constitute approval for the pilot to execute a contact approach or a visual approach to the airport or runway.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(b), what is the authorised DA/DH or MDA?
notes.back: The highest of: the one the procedure prescribes, the one prescribed for the pilot in command, and the one suited to the equipment used.
notes.explanation: Whichever of the three is most restrictive sets the minimum for that approach.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: the authorized DA/DH or MDA is the highest of the following: (1) The DA/DH or MDA prescribed by the approach procedure. (2) The DA/DH or MDA prescribed for the pilot in command. (3) The DA/DH or MDA appropriate for the aircraft equipment available and used during the approach.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What speed places an aeroplane in an approach category?
notes.back: Its reference landing speed at maximum certified landing weight or, if none is specified, 1.3 × VS0 at that weight.
notes.explanation: The values are those set by the certification authority of the country of registry.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Aircraft approach category means a grouping of aircraft based on a speed of VREF at the maximum certified landing weight, if specified, or if VREF is not specified, 1.3VSO at the maximum certified landing weight. VREF, VSO, and the maximum certified landing weight are those values as established for the aircraft by the certification authority of the country of registry.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What speed range defines approach Category A?
notes.back: Less than 91 knots.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest band in a table that rises from A to E as the speed increases.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Category A: Speed less than 91 knots. Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots. Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots. Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots. Category E: Speed 166 knots or more.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aeroplane's category speed is 105 knots. Which approach category is it in?
notes.back: Category B (91 knots or more but less than 121).
notes.explanation: Category B picks up where Category A stops, at 91 knots.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Category A: Speed less than 91 knots. Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots. Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots. Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots. Category E: Speed 166 knots or more.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What speed range defines approach Category C?
notes.back: 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots.
notes.explanation: It starts where Category B ends, at 121 knots.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Category A: Speed less than 91 knots. Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots. Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots. Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots. Category E: Speed 166 knots or more.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aeroplane's category speed is 150 knots. Which approach category is it in?
notes.back: Category D (141 knots or more but less than 166).
notes.explanation: Category D starts at 141 knots and stops short of Category E's 166 knots.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Category A: Speed less than 91 knots. Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots. Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots. Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots. Category E: Speed 166 knots or more.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: From what speed does approach Category E begin?
notes.back: 166 knots.
notes.explanation: It is open-ended: every speed from 166 knots upwards.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Category A: Speed less than 91 knots. Category B: Speed 91 knots or more but less than 121 knots. Category C: Speed 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots. Category D: Speed 141 knots or more but less than 166 knots. Category E: Speed 166 knots or more.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If it is necessary to fly faster than the upper limit of the aircraft's category speed range, which minimums should be used?
notes.back: The minimums for the higher category.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual names heavy or gusty wind, icing and non-normal conditions as cases where this may happen.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: If it is necessary to operate at a speed in excess of the upper limit of the speed range for an aircraft's category, the minimums for the higher category should be used. This may occur with certain aircraft types operating in heavy/gusty wind, icing, or non-normal conditions.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Is a momentary descent below DA allowed while changing to the missed approach?
notes.back: Yes; obstacle clearance allows for a momentary descent below DA during that transition.
notes.explanation: The missed approach is then flown along the final course to at least the runway threshold waypoint or missed approach point before turning.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Obstacle clearance is provided to allow a momentary descent below DA while transitioning from the final approach to the missed approach. The aircraft is expected to follow the missed instructions while continuing along the published final approach course to at least the published runway threshold waypoint or MAP (if not at the threshold) before executing any turns.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The height above touchdown for a CAT I precision approach is normally {{c1::200 feet}} above touchdown zone elevation.
notes.back: 200 feet.
notes.explanation: HAT is measured from the touchdown zone, so this figure is a height, not the altitude printed as the DA.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Approach Minimums, PDF page 20
notes.evidence: approach is normally 200 feet above touchdown zone
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Name two area navigation lines of minima that the Aeronautical Information Manual classes as approaches with vertical guidance?
notes.back: LNAV/VNAV and LPV.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual's examples also include barometric vertical navigation.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: For example, Baro-VNAV, LDA with glidepath, LNAV/VNAV and LPV are APV approaches.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An LNAV approach publishes a vertical descent angle. Does that make it an approach with vertical guidance?
notes.back: No; it must still be flown to an MDA.
notes.explanation: The angle was never evaluated as a glidepath, so the minimum stays an MDA.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: This does not make the approach an APV procedure, since it must still be flown to an MDA and has not been evaluated with a glidepath.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: To what kind of minimum is an LPV approach flown?
notes.back: A decision altitude, as with an ILS.
notes.explanation: Vertical guidance is what gives it a DA instead of an MDA.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Just as with an ILS, the LPV has vertical guidance and is flown to a DA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Why are LNAV/VNAV minimums published as a DA?
notes.back: Because electronic vertical guidance is provided.
notes.explanation: Aircraft using the line descend on an internally generated path from satellite or approved barometric systems.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Aircraft using LNAV/VNAV minimums will descend to landing via an internally generated descent path based on satellite or other approach approved VNAV systems. Since electronic vertical guidance is provided, the minima will be published as a DA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Is an LP line of minima a DA or an MDA?
notes.back: An MDA.
notes.explanation: However precise, LP guidance is lateral only, so its minimum is a descent altitude.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: However, the LP line of minima is a Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA) rather than a DA (H).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Is LP a fail-down mode for LPV?
notes.back: No; LP is published only where terrain, obstructions or some other reason prevent a vertically guided procedure.
notes.explanation: LP is a separate line for runways that cannot have vertical guidance, not a fallback from LPV.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: LP is not a fail-down mode for LPV. LP will only be published if terrain, obstructions, or some other reason prevent publishing a vertically guided procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Once an approach is active, does a WAAS receiver drop to a lower level of service by itself?
notes.back: No; if only the vertical off flag appears, the pilot may elect LNAV minima where the operating rules allow.
notes.explanation: Changing to LNAV is a pilot decision, not something the receiver does itself.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 1-1-18 Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)
notes.evidence: Receivers do not “fail down” to lower levels of service once the approach has been activated. If only the vertical off flag appears, the pilot may elect to use the LNAV minima if the rules under which the flight is operating allow changing the type of approach being flown after commencing the procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When an approach is selected and active, what level of service does a WAAS receiver announce?
notes.back: The most accurate level supported by the WAAS signal, the receiver and the selected approach together.
notes.explanation: The announcement uses the chart's own names for the lines of minima, such as LPV or LNAV.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 1-1-18 Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)
notes.evidence: When an approach procedure is selected and active, the receiver will notify the pilot of the most accurate level of service supported by the combination of the WAAS signal, the receiver, and the selected approach, using the naming conventions on the minima lines of the selected approach procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May the pilot descend below the MDA before reaching the VDP?
notes.back: The pilot should not.
notes.explanation: The VDP is where a stabilised visual descent from the MDA is designed to begin.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: The pilot should not descend below the MDA prior to reaching the VDP.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On area navigation approaches, to which lines of minima do VDPs apply?
notes.back: LP and LNAV only, not LPV or LNAV/VNAV.
notes.explanation: Both of those lines end at an MDA, the altitude a VDP descent starts from.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: VDPs apply only to aircraft utilizing LP or LNAV minima, not LPV or LNAV/VNAV minimums.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What rate of descent does the Instrument Procedures Handbook call unacceptable in the final stages of an approach, below 1,000 feet above ground?
notes.back: More than approximately 1,000 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: The handbook applies this to the final stages, when the aircraft is close to the ground.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Maximum Acceptable Descent Rates, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: descent rate of greater than approximately 1,000 fpm is
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the Instrument Procedures Handbook work out the descent rate from the FAF on a nonprecision approach?
notes.back: Subtract the touchdown zone elevation from the FAF altitude and divide by the time inbound.
notes.explanation: Dividing the height to lose by the time available gives one steady rate to fly.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: rate of descent, subtract the TDZE from the FAF altitude
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: To check an approximate three-degree glidepath, the handbook uses {{c1::300 feet}} per nautical mile from the threshold.
notes.back: 300 feet.
notes.explanation: It is a quick cross-check of height against distance to see whether the aircraft is near a normal glidepath.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: use a calculation of 300 feet to 1 NM.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When must an RVR minimum be converted to ground visibility?
notes.back: When RVR minimums are prescribed in the approach procedure but RVR is not reported for that runway.
notes.explanation: The converted figure then becomes the visibility minimum for that runway.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(1)
notes.evidence: if RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are prescribed in an instrument approach procedure, but RVR is not reported for the runway of intended operation, the RVR minimum shall be converted to ground visibility in accordance with the table in paragraph (h)(2) of this section and shall be the visibility minimum for takeoff or landing on that runway.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 1,600 feet convert to?
notes.back: 1/4 statute mile.
notes.explanation: 1,600 feet is the lowest entry in the conversion table.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 2,400 feet convert to?
notes.back: 1/2 statute mile.
notes.explanation: It is the second entry in the table, one step above 1,600 feet.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 3,200 feet convert to?
notes.back: 5/8 statute mile.
notes.explanation: It sits between the 2,400 foot (1/2 mile) and 4,000 foot (3/4 mile) entries.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 4,000 feet convert to?
notes.back: 3/4 statute mile.
notes.explanation: It follows the 3,200 foot entry, which converts to 5/8 mile.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 4,500 feet convert to?
notes.back: 7/8 statute mile.
notes.explanation: It is the step between 3/4 mile at 4,000 feet and 1 mile at 5,000 feet.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which RVR value in the 91.175(h) table converts to 1 statute mile?
notes.back: 5,000 feet.
notes.explanation: It is the only entry that converts to a whole mile.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.175(h), what ground visibility does an RVR of 6,000 feet convert to?
notes.back: 1 1/4 statute miles.
notes.explanation: 6,000 feet is the highest entry in the conversion table.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (h)(2)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What airborne radio equipment does a radar approach require?
notes.back: Only a functioning radio transmitter and receiver.
notes.explanation: The radar controller does the navigating, vectoring the aircraft onto the runway centreline.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-11 Radar Approaches
notes.evidence: The only airborne radio equipment required for radar approaches is a functioning radio transmitter and receiver. The radar controller vectors the aircraft to align it with the runway centerline.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a no-gyro approach, how should the pilot turn, and what changes after turning onto final?
notes.back: At standard rate, as soon as instructed; on final of a surveillance or precision approach, at half standard rate once told.
notes.explanation: The controller steers with 'turn right' and 'stop turn' calls instead of headings.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-11 Radar Approaches
notes.evidence: The pilot should make all turns at standard rate and should execute the turn immediately upon receipt of instructions. For example, “TURN RIGHT,” “STOP TURN.” When a surveillance or precision approach is made, the pilot will be advised after the aircraft has been turned onto final approach to make turns at half standard rate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: To what kind of minimum is a side-step manoeuvre flown?
notes.back: An MDA, whatever approach was authorised.
notes.explanation: Side-step minimums use nonprecision criteria, so they are higher than precision minimums to the primary runway but normally below circling minimums.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-19 Side-step Maneuver
notes.evidence: Side-step minima are flown to a Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA) regardless of the approach authorized. Landing minimums to the adjacent runway will be based on nonprecision criteria and therefore higher than the precision minimums to the primary runway, but will normally be lower than the published circling minimums.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Once cleared for a simultaneous parallel approach, what must each pilot keep to?
notes.back: The lateral and vertical path of the procedure, unless ATC instructs otherwise.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual says parallel approach operations demand heightened situational awareness.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-13 Simultaneous Approaches to Parallel Runways
notes.evidence: Parallel approach operations demand heightened pilot situational awareness. Once cleared for an approach procedure, each pilot must maintain the lateral and vertical path of the procedure unless otherwise instructed by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Cleared to 'descend via' an arrival, a pilot at FL 200 wonders when to leave that level. What may the pilot do?
notes.back: A) Descend at own discretion, meeting every published restriction.
notes.choices:
A) Descend at own discretion, meeting every published restriction
B) Stay level until ATC assigns an altitude
C) Descend straight to the lowest altitude on the arrival
notes.choicesExplained: B: the descend via clearance already authorises the descent. C: each published restriction on the way down must still be met.
notes.explanation: The clearance leaves the timing to the pilot and the profile to the chart.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: Descend at pilot's discretion to meet published restrictions and laterally navigate on a STAR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a STAR, ATC gives a pilot a new altitude but says nothing about speed. A published speed restriction lies ahead. What applies?
notes.back: B) The published speed restriction still applies.
notes.choices:
A) Only "expect" speeds now apply
B) The published speed restriction still applies
C) All speed restrictions lapse with the altitude change
notes.choicesExplained: A: 'expect' values are for planning and bind only if ATC issues them. C: speed restrictions are independent of altitude restrictions.
notes.explanation: Only ATC can modify a published STAR speed, and an altitude instruction does not do so.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-1 Standard Terminal Arrival (STAR) Procedures
notes.evidence: Published speed restrictions are independent of altitude restrictions and are mandatory unless modified by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aircraft has just crossed the final approach fix inbound on a nonprecision approach. Which segment is it in?
notes.back: C) Final approach segment.
notes.choices:
A) Intermediate approach segment
B) Initial approach segment
C) Final approach segment
notes.choicesExplained: A: the intermediate segment ends at the FAF. B: the initial segment ends at the intermediate fix or course.
notes.explanation: Part 97 starts the final segment at the final approach fix and ends it at the runway, airport or missed approach point.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Final approach is the segment between the final approach fix or point and the runway, airport, or missed approach point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Weather at a civil airport requires an instrument approach. A pilot plans a self-built GPS track to the runway instead of the published procedure, with no FAA authorisation. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the pilot is instrument current
B) No
C) Yes, if ATC provides radar monitoring
notes.choicesExplained: A: currency does not replace the requirement for a part 97 procedure. C: radar monitoring is not an FAA authorisation to depart from part 97.
notes.explanation: Unless the FAA authorises otherwise, a necessary instrument approach to a civil airport must use the part 97 procedure.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized by the FAA, when it is necessary to use an instrument approach to a civil airport, each person operating an aircraft must use a standard instrument approach procedure prescribed in part 97 of this chapter for that airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: ATC vectors a pilot to the final approach course of an approach whose chart shows a procedure turn. Should the pilot fly the procedure turn?
notes.back: C) No, not unless ATC clears it.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if still above the procedure turn altitude
B) Yes, because it is depicted
C) No, not unless ATC clears it
notes.choicesExplained: A: altitude does not change the rule; only an ATC clearance does. B: a radar vector to final removes the procedure turn despite the depiction.
notes.explanation: Section 91.175(j) bars the procedure turn after a radar vector to the final approach course unless ATC clears it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (j)
notes.evidence: In the case of a radar vector to a final approach course or fix, a timed approach from a holding fix, or an approach for which the procedure specifies “No PT,” no pilot may make a procedure turn unless cleared to do so by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying to an IAF that has a published procedure turn, a pilot is cleared for the approach with no mention of straight-in. What next?
notes.back: C) Fly the procedure turn and complete the approach.
notes.choices:
A) Turn straight onto final at the IAF
B) Hold at the IAF until ATC says more
C) Fly the procedure turn and complete the approach
notes.choicesExplained: A: going straight in needs a straight-in approach clearance. B: the approach clearance already covers the course reversal.
notes.explanation: Without a straight-in clearance, the published course reversal is part of the approach the pilot was cleared for.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-6 Approach Clearance
notes.evidence: If proceeding to an IAF with a published course reversal (procedure turn or hold-in-lieu of PT pattern), except when cleared for a straight in approach by ATC, the pilot must execute the procedure turn/hold-in-lieu of PT, and complete the approach.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aircraft cleared for an area navigation approach enters a TAA sector labelled NoPT. What should the pilot do at the dual-purpose intermediate fix?
notes.back: A) Continue straight in without a course reversal.
notes.choices:
A) Continue straight in without a course reversal
B) Fly the hold in lieu of procedure turn first
C) Hold until ATC assigns an altitude
notes.choicesExplained: B: the course reversal must not be flown in a NoPT sector. C: the approach clearance already allows the approach to continue.
notes.explanation: A NoPT label on the sector removes the course reversal for aircraft arriving from it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: Pilots must not execute the HILPT course reversal when the sector or procedure segment is labeled “NoPT.”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
uses: hold in lieu of procedure turn

notes.front: Vectored at 3,000 feet and cleared for the approach, a pilot sees 2,200 feet charted on the segment ahead, not yet joined. What altitude now?
notes.back: C) Keep 3,000 feet until established on the published segment.
notes.choices:
A) Descend to the MDA
B) Descend to 2,200 feet at once
C) Keep 3,000 feet until established on the published segment
notes.choicesExplained: A: the MDA applies on final, not while being vectored. B: charted segment altitudes apply only once established on that segment.
notes.explanation: The last assigned altitude stays in force until the aircraft is on a published segment.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: maintain the last assigned altitude unless a different altitude is assigned by ATC, or until the aircraft is established on a segment of a published route or IAP.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot is cleared for 'ILS runway 9 approach, glideslope unusable'. What does this tell the pilot?
notes.back: B) The approach keeps its name, but the glideslope must not be used.
notes.choices:
A) The approach is cancelled
B) The approach keeps its name, but the glideslope must not be used
C) The glideslope may be used down to 1,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: the controller still clears the published approach. C: an unusable component is not to be used at all.
notes.explanation: The controller must name the approach as published and say which component is unusable.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-6 Approach Clearance
notes.evidence: The controller will use the name of the approach as published, but must advise the aircraft at the time an approach clearance is issued that the inoperative or unreliable approach aid component is unusable
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An approach's MDA is 1,200 feet. The minimums prescribed for this pilot in command are 1,300 feet; the equipment used allows 1,200. What is the authorised MDA?
notes.back: B) 1,300 feet.
notes.choices:
A) 1,200 feet
B) 1,300 feet
C) 1,250 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: the lower figure is not the highest of the three. C: the rule takes the highest value, not an average.
notes.explanation: Section 91.175(b) takes the highest of the procedure, pilot and equipment minimums.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 Takeoff and landing under IFR (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: the authorized DA/DH or MDA is the highest of the following: (1) The DA/DH or MDA prescribed by the approach procedure. (2) The DA/DH or MDA prescribed for the pilot in command.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aeroplane has no reference landing speed specified; 1.3 × VS0 at maximum certified landing weight is 88 knots. Which approach category is it?
notes.back: B) Category A.
notes.choices:
A) It depends on the landing weight on the day
B) Category A
C) Category B
notes.choicesExplained: A: the category is fixed at maximum certified landing weight, not the actual weight. C: Category B starts at 91 knots.
notes.explanation: With no reference speed, 1.3 × VS0 at maximum certified landing weight sets the category, and 88 knots is below 91.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: Aircraft approach category means a grouping of aircraft based on a speed of VREF at the maximum certified landing weight, if specified, or if VREF is not specified, 1.3VSO at the maximum certified landing weight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A Category B aeroplane must circle to land at 145 knots because of gusty wind. Which minimums should it use?
notes.back: B) Category D.
notes.choices:
A) Category B
B) Category D
C) Category C
notes.choicesExplained: A: its own category no longer matches the speed flown. C: Category C ends below 141 knots, so 145 knots falls in D.
notes.explanation: Flying faster than the category range means using the category that matches the speed.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-7 Instrument Approach Procedures
notes.evidence: If it is necessary to operate at a speed in excess of the upper limit of the speed range for an aircraft's category, the minimums for the higher category should be used. This may occur with certain aircraft types operating in heavy/gusty wind, icing, or non-normal conditions.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying an LPV approach, the altimeter reaches the DA and the pilot does not see the required visual reference. What now?
notes.back: A) Start an immediate missed approach.
notes.choices:
A) Start an immediate missed approach
B) Level off and continue to the missed approach point
C) Descend 100 feet and look again
notes.choicesExplained: B: a DA is a decision point, not a level to fly along. C: no further descent is allowed without the required reference.
notes.explanation: At the DA, lacking the reference, the definition calls for an immediate missed approach.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Decision altitude (DA) is a specified altitude in an instrument approach procedure at which the pilot must decide whether to initiate an immediate missed approach if the pilot does not see the required visual reference, or to continue the approach. Decision altitude is expressed in feet above mean sea level.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A number on an approach chart gives the height of a minimum above the runway touchdown zone, not above sea level. What is it?
notes.back: B) Height above touchdown.
notes.choices:
A) Minimum descent altitude
B) Height above touchdown
C) Decision altitude
notes.choicesExplained: A: an MDA is also expressed above mean sea level. C: a DA is an altitude above mean sea level.
notes.explanation: HAT is measured from the touchdown zone, while DA and MDA are altitudes.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 97.3 Symbols and terms used in procedures (eCFR)
notes.evidence: HAT means height above touchdown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under section 1.1 of the regulations, how is an ILS approach classed?
notes.back: B) Precision approach procedure.
notes.choices:
A) Approach with vertical guidance
B) Precision approach procedure
C) Nonprecision approach procedure
notes.choicesExplained: A: APV is the Aeronautical Information Manual class for guidance that is not held to the precision standard. C: an ILS provides an electronic glide slope.
notes.explanation: Section 1.1 names the ILS as an example of a procedure with an electronic glide slope.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Precision approach procedure means a standard instrument approach procedure in which an electronic glide slope is provided, such as ILS and PAR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the Aeronautical Information Manual's approach types, how is an approach to LPV minimums classed?
notes.back: A) Approach with vertical guidance.
notes.choices:
A) Approach with vertical guidance
B) Precision approach
C) Nonprecision approach
notes.choicesExplained: B: LPV is not required to meet the precision standard. C: LPV gives vertical as well as lateral guidance.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual lists LPV among its APV examples.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: For example, Baro-VNAV, LDA with glidepath, LNAV/VNAV and LPV are APV approaches.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An area navigation chart shows LPV, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV lines of minima. Which is flown to an MDA?
notes.back: A) LNAV.
notes.choices:
A) LNAV
B) LPV
C) LNAV/VNAV
notes.choicesExplained: B: LPV is flown to a DA, like an ILS. C: LNAV/VNAV has electronic vertical guidance and a DA.
notes.explanation: The LNAV line is lateral guidance only, so its minimum is published as an MDA.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: LNAV. This minima is for lateral navigation only, and the approach minimum altitude will be published as a minimum descent altitude (MDA).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A chart's line of minima reads 'LP MDA'. What kind of guidance does it give?
notes.back: A) Lateral only.
notes.choices:
A) Lateral only
B) Vertical only
C) Lateral and vertical
notes.choicesExplained: C: LP is published only where a vertically guided procedure cannot be, and it has no glidepath. B: LP is a lateral guidance line.
notes.explanation: LP is published where vertical guidance cannot be provided, and its minimum is an MDA.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: LP will only be published if terrain, obstructions, or some other reason prevent publishing a vertically guided procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: During an approach to LPV minimums, only the vertical guidance flag appears; lateral guidance is normal. What may the pilot do?
notes.back: C) Use LNAV minima, if the operating rules allow changing approach type.
notes.choices:
A) Wait for the receiver to switch to LNAV/VNAV
B) Continue to the LPV DA
C) Use LNAV minima, if the operating rules allow changing approach type
notes.choicesExplained: B: the LPV DA depends on the vertical guidance that has failed. A: receivers do not fail down by themselves once the approach is active.
notes.explanation: The switch to LNAV is the pilot's choice, limited by the rules the flight is operating under.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 1-1-18 Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)
notes.evidence: If only the vertical off flag appears, the pilot may elect to use the LNAV minima if the rules under which the flight is operating allow changing the type of approach being flown after commencing the procedure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Level at the MDA on an LNAV approach, a pilot sees the runway lights well before the charted VDP. What should the pilot do?
notes.back: C) Stay at the MDA until the VDP.
notes.choices:
A) Climb and go missed
B) Start down at once
C) Stay at the MDA until the VDP
notes.choicesExplained: A: having the runway in sight is no reason to miss. B: descent below the MDA should wait for the VDP.
notes.explanation: The VDP is where the stabilised visual descent is meant to start.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: The pilot should not descend below the MDA prior to reaching the VDP.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The FAF altitude is 2,600 feet, the touchdown zone elevation 600 feet and the time inbound 2 minutes. What descent rate does the handbook method give?
notes.back: B) 1,000 feet per minute.
notes.choices:
A) 1,300 feet per minute
B) 1,000 feet per minute
C) 800 feet per minute
notes.choicesExplained: A: that divides the FAF altitude alone by the time, ignoring the touchdown zone elevation. C: 800 feet per minute for 2 minutes loses only 1,600 of the 2,000 feet.
notes.explanation: Height to lose is 2,600 minus 600, or 2,000 feet; over 2 minutes that is 1,000 feet per minute.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: rate of descent, subtract the TDZE from the FAF altitude
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At 800 feet above ground on final, a pilot is descending at 1,400 feet per minute to regain the path. How does the handbook judge this?
notes.back: B) Unacceptable for the final stages of an approach.
notes.choices:
A) Acceptable while on course
B) Unacceptable for the final stages of an approach
C) Acceptable until 500 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A: being on course does not make the descent rate acceptable. C: the handbook applies the limit below 1,000 feet, not 500.
notes.explanation: The handbook treats more than about 1,000 feet per minute below 1,000 feet above ground as unacceptable.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Maximum Acceptable Descent Rates, PDF page 37
notes.evidence: descent rate of greater than approximately 1,000 fpm is
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An approach needs RVR 3,000, but RVR is not reported for the runway. Using the Aeronautical Information Manual method, what visibility minimum applies?
notes.back: B) 5/8 mile.
notes.choices:
A) 9/16 mile
B) 5/8 mile
C) 1/2 mile
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Aeronautical Information Manual says not to interpolate. C: that is the value for 2,400, the lower entry.
notes.explanation: For a value between table entries, the Aeronautical Information Manual says to use the next higher RVR, here 3,200.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-20 Approach and Landing Minimums
notes.evidence: For converting RVR values that fall between listed values, use the next higher RVR value; do not interpolate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the difference between a decision altitude and a decision height?
notes.back: A DA is expressed in feet above mean sea level; a DH in feet above ground level.
notes.explanation: Both mark the same continue-or-miss decision; only the reference level differs.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Decision altitude is expressed in feet above mean sea level. Decision height (DH) is a specified height above the ground in an instrument approach procedure at which the pilot must decide whether to initiate an immediate missed approach
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under section 1.1 of the regulations, is an approach to LPV minimums a precision approach procedure?
notes.back: No; section 1.1 requires an electronic glide slope, such as an ILS. LPV is classed as an approach with vertical guidance.
notes.explanation: LPV has a glidepath, but the regulation reserves "precision" for procedures with an electronic glide slope.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Precision approach procedure means a standard instrument approach procedure in which an electronic glide slope is provided, such as ILS and PAR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When LP and LNAV lines both appear on one chart, what does that tell you about LP?
notes.back: That LP gives lower minima, since LP is only published if it does.
notes.explanation: Both lines are lateral-only; the chart carries LP only when it improves on LNAV.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, 5-4-5 Instrument Approach Procedure (IAP) Charts
notes.evidence: It is possible to have LP and LNAV published on the same approach chart but LP will only be published if it provides lower minima than an LNAV line of minima.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
